item.title: Spatiotemporal Landslide Runout Reconstruction from Sparse Observations with LAPIS-SHRED
item.description: arXiv:2611.27132v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of landslide runout from limited observations is a central challenge in geohazard assessment: transient flow dynamics are rarely observed directly, and available data are often confined to post-event deposits or brief monitoring windows. We apply LAPIS-SHRED (LAtent Phase Inference from Short time sequence using SHallow REcurrent Decoders) to reconstruct runout events near Mount St. Helens, USA. Trained on physics-based simulation ensembles, the framework supports both backward reconstruction from single frame and forward prediction from short initial window across different runout regimes. Using 32 sensor observations from a single timepoint, LAPIS-SHRED recovers complete runout trajectories with NRMSE below 5.8%, robust across varying observational and training conditions. Validation against observed deposits yields spatial correlation of r = 0.843 against the calibrated simulator's r = 0.853. These results suggest that latent-space temporal inference offers a viable pathway for spatiotemporal landslide reconstruction under extreme observational constraints typical of field settings.
item.dc:creator: Xingyue Zhang, Yuxuan Bao, Jeffrey Keck, Erkan Istanbulluoglu, J. Nathan Kutz

item.title: Long-Term Stable Three-Axis Single-Beam Alignment-Based Atomic Magnetometer Using an Uncoated Buffer-Gas-Free Rubidium Ampoule for Unshielded Geomagnetic Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.12905v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optically pumped magnetometers achieve exceptional sensitivity, yet sustaining long-term baseline stability in unshielded Earth-field environments (~50,000 nT) remains challenging. We present the design, quantum-interference principles, calibration, and unshielded validation of a three-axis single-beam alignment-based atomic magnetometer built from an unmodified, uncoated, buffer-gas-free commercial rubidium (Rb) ampoule and a single 795 nm VCSEL. Pumped with $45^\circ$-oriented linearly polarized light on the $^{87}$Rb $D_1$ ($F=2 \to F'=1$) transition, the sensor exploits ground-state Zeeman quantum interference (rank-2 spin alignment), intrinsically cancelling first-order vector light shifts. Dual-zone 20 kHz AC heating ($75.0^\circ$C lower liquid Rb reservoir, $85.0^\circ$C upper optical zone) suppresses window condensation and thermal magnetic gradients over 29 days. Without buffer-gas pressure broadening, the VCSEL is stabilized via direct absorption spectroscopy at an optimized 3530 Hz dither frequency, eliminating odd-harmonic intermodulation leakage. A hybrid balanced polarimeter extracts $B_x$, $B_y$, and laser-lock errors from total absorption (sum channel) and $B_z$ from alignment-induced linear dichroism (difference channel) within an active zero-field compensation loop using a 12-bit microcontroller in a dual-stage mid-ranging architecture. Spectral analysis yields sub-LSB noise amplitudes of 0.5-5 pT at 1 Hz (15-150 $\mathrm{pT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$), rolling off to 0.1-1 pT (3-30 $\mathrm{pT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$) near 10 Hz. Continuous unshielded geomagnetic monitoring in Okayama benchmarked against synthesized Kakioka and Kanoya observatory records demonstrates high tracking fidelity and bounds instrumental bias instability to $\le 0.1$ nT at 100-200 s integration times.
item.dc:creator: Minaru Kawamura

item.title: Sulfur photochemistry traces mantle redox states of rocky planets
item.description: arXiv:2607.15204v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Volatile outgassing from planetary interiors controls the composition of rocky exoplanets' secondary atmospheres. However, observations indicate that disequilibrium processes can strongly alter the chemical structure of hot Jupiters. How outgassing and photochemistry jointly determine the resulting atmospheric composition remains an open question. Sulfur-bearing species are promising tracers of interior-atmosphere coupling because their atmospheric abundances are sensitive to both mantle redox state and stellar irradiation. We investigate how photochemistry modifies outgassed atmospheres of diverse Earth-sized worlds during the magma ocean phase and assess how sulfur traces the interior oxidation state. The PROTEUS planetary interior-atmosphere evolution modelling framework is coupled to two chemical models, FastChem and VULCAN. We ran a grid of planetary evolution simulations spanning diverse mantle redox states, instellation fluxes, and host-star spectra. For each case, we compared atmospheric compositions with three post-processing calculations: thermochemical equilibrium, with disequilibrium vertical transport and with vertical transport plus photochemistry. The bulk atmospheric composition remains controlled by the mantle redox state and the history of outgassing. Reduced mantles produce atmospheres rich in H2 and CH4 and oxidised mantles are dominated by CO2 and H2O. Photochemistry affects the low-pressure upper atmosphere, strongly depleting neutral volatiles and enhancing radicals. Synthetic emission spectra show that photochemical SO2 can generate absorption features at 4 um and at 7.3/8.7 um, reaching ~60 ppm and ~100 ppm, respectively, before sequentially returning to the outgassed signatures of ~30 ppm and ~50 ppm for the oxidised mantle redox state. These signatures are potentially detectable with JWST, motivating targeted observational campaigns.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Panagiotou, Tim Lichtenberg, Shang-Min Tsai, Harrison Nicholls
